deeds.name: Fulfil bounties
deeds.text: the bounties the heroes have brought home

deeds.name: Throw back raids and assaults
deeds.text: the town standing firm against its foes

deeds.name: See menaces ended
deeds.text: a menace gone from the map

deeds.name: Keep the town content
deeds.text: a long stretch of contented folk

feats.name: Inspiring Leader
feats.text: Hold one more Inspiration, and gain one now.

feats.name: Practised Hand
feats.text: On skills you are trained in, a d20 under 6 counts as a 6. No natural 1s.

feats.name: Cool Head
feats.text: A miss within 5 of the DC is a success at a cost, where a choice allows one.

motion.success: The hall comes round to the mayor's view (+1 Mandate).
motion.failure: The hall grumbles, but goes along.

submit.success: The mayor kneels without grovelling, and the town respects it (+3 Mandate).

refuse.success: The answer gives the foe pause; some of its followers slip away.

envoy.success: The mayor's own letter goes down well (+4 standing).

crackdown.success: The mayor faces the crooks down in person (+1 Mandate).

backgrounds.name: Disgraced councillor
backgrounds.text: You sat on a League town's council until a scandal. You know how a chamber turns, and you have advantage on checks in council stories.

backgrounds.name: Soldier
backgrounds.text: You stood in a League levy when the beacons were lit. Fighters listen to you, and you have advantage on checks in war stories.

backgrounds.name: Acolyte
backgrounds.text: You lit the beacon-lamps at a League temple. The faithful trust you, and you have advantage on checks in stories of faith.

backgrounds.name: Sage
backgrounds.text: You copied Caldor's old records for the Unshut Book. Old things speak to you, and you have advantage on checks in stories of the old world.

backgrounds.name: Toll collector
backgrounds.text: You kept the tolls on a League road and missed nothing. You have advantage on checks in the town's own troubles.

backgrounds.name: Caravan guard
backgrounds.text: You rode guard on the Oasis road. You know weather and wild country, and you have advantage on checks in stories from the road.

backgrounds.name: Criminal
backgrounds.text: You learned the trade on the wharves of the Free Ports, and you still know who to ask. You have advantage on checks in stories of the factions.

stages.text: Two caravan hands and a militiaman off duty are trading punches over a game of knucklebones, and half of {tavern} has taken sides.

options.label: Wade in and pull them apart

success.text: You haul the loudest of them out by the collar, and the room cheers.

partial.text: You break it up, but a table and two benches don't survive it.

failure.text: You end up on the floor with ale in your hair. People will tell that one for weeks.

success.text: The room goes quiet at the mayor's voice, and the brawlers sit down sheepishly.

failure.text: Nobody hears you over the noise. The watch clears the room at midnight.

options.label: Buy a round for the house

success.text: Nothing ends a fight like free ale.

ignored.text: The watch drags them out by dawn. Someone's tooth is still under a table.

stages.text: A smiling stranger has won at three-dragon every night this week, and the losers say his deck has more dragons than it should.

success.text: You catch the card in his sleeve. His winnings go back to the town.

failure.text: You see nothing amiss. He tips his hat to you on his way out.

options.label: Read the man, not the cards

success.text: One look tells you he's lying. Faced with it, he pays back the worst of his marks and leaves.

failure.text: He seems an honest sort to you. The losers disagree.

critical.text: You cheat the cheat, and he leaves town with his pockets turned out.

success.text: You beat him at his own game, to roars from the tables.

failure.text: He takes you for a purse of the town's gold, and smiles while he does it.

fumble.text: He takes you for everything you brought, and the whole tavern saw it.

ignored.text: He leaves on the morning cart with a purse full of {town}'s coin.

stages.text: {hero} has bet a crowd at the well that nobody in {town} can out-wrestle them, and the crowd is calling for the mayor.

success.text: You pin {heroName} in the mud to cheers. They laugh and buy you a drink.

partial.text: You last longer than anyone thought, and {heroName} claps you on the back.

failure.text: {heroName} throws you in the trough, then helps you out, grinning.

success.text: Your toast to {town}'s champions has the crowd stamping. {heroName} goes red to the ears.

failure.text: The toast falls flat, and {heroName} wanders off.

success.text: The crowd breaks up. {heroName} sulks, but does as you say.

failure.text: {heroName} laughs in your face and the crowd laughs with them.

ignored.text: Nobody takes the wager. {heroName} grumbles that this town has no sport in it.

stages.text: {hero} has been seen buying rope and rations, and the word at the inn is that they mean to leave for a town that pays better.

options.label: Remind them what the town owes them

success.text: You talk until the candles gutter. {heroName} unpacks.

partial.text: {heroName} stays, for now, and for a little gold.

failure.text: {heroName} hears you out and says nothing. The pack stays by the door.

options.label: Find out what is really wrong

success.text: It isn't the pay. It's that nobody thanked them for the last one. You do.

failure.text: You guess wrong, and {heroName} is offended.

options.label: Send a purse to their room

success.text: Gold talks. {heroName} stays.

ignored.text: Nobody from the hall comes. {heroName} takes it as an answer.

stages.text: The sending stone at the hall cracks with a voice: {party} is pinned by a storm far out in the wilds, and {hero} asks whether to press on or turn back.

options.label: Read the weather and guide them

critical.text: You call every turn of the storm right. {heroName} swears {town} has a weather-witch for a mayor.

success.text: They come through the storm on your word, and {heroName} won't forget it.

failure.text: Your advice takes them into the teeth of it. They come through, but it costs them.

options.label: Find a safe road on the old maps

success.text: An old road of the drovers runs in the lee of the ridge. They find it.

failure.text: The old road is long gone under the scree.

success.text: They sit it out in a cave, and come on when the sky clears.

failure.text: Holding fast means three cold nights with too little food.

ignored.text: The stone stays silent. When they come home, {heroName} asks why nobody answered.

stages.text: {councillor}, the {seat}, has called a fellow councillor a thief in open session, and both refuse to sit until the other apologises.

success.text: A shared jug, a long night and a handshake. The council sits again.

partial.text: They sit again, glaring at each other across the table.

failure.text: Your peace lasts until the first vote.

critical.text: The accounts don't lie: a fat purse was skimmed, and every coin of it comes back.

success.text: There was a thief, and the gold comes back. {councillor} was right, and insufferable about it.

failure.text: You find nothing, and both of them feel accused.

success.text: They go back to work, sullen but quiet.

failure.text: {councillor} walks out of the chamber, and half the town hears why.

ignored.text: The feud festers, and the town's business waits on it.

stages.text: A messenger brings a sealed letter from {faction}: their people will be at the town's service, for a seat at your table and a blind eye now and then.

success.text: You get their help and a gift for the treasury, and give them very little.

failure.text: They think you greedy, and go away to think again.

success.text: You shake on it. Some in town mutter about the company you keep.
The messenger leaves pale, and the town hears that its mayor can't be bought.

failure.text: They laugh at the threat, and remember it.

ignored.text: No answer comes from the hall, and the silence is taken as an insult by {faction}.

stages.text: The watch has caught someone copying the treasury's books by candlelight. Under the ink on their fingers is the mark of {faction}.

success.text: They talk, and the fine for their release is paid in full by {faction}.

failure.text: They say nothing at all, and are gone from the cells by morning.

options.label: Turn them, and feed {faction} false books

critical.text: Every false figure is believed, and {faction} is made a laughing stock.

success.text: The spy goes home with books that lead {faction} nowhere, and the fine is paid twice over.

failure.text: The spy sees through you, and every word of it goes back to {faction}.

options.label: Let them go with a warning

success.text: The courtesy is not lost on {faction}. The town is less pleased.

ignored.text: The spy is sprung from the cells in the night, and the books go with them.

stages.text: A rider under a filthy white rag waits at the ford. {menace} wants to talk about who the valleys belong to.

success.text: You learn more from what the envoy won't say than from what they do, and the heroes hear all of it.

failure.text: The envoy learns more about {town} than you do about them.

success.text: The envoy rides off sure the town has twice the walls it has. {menace} turns its eyes elsewhere a while.

failure.text: The envoy smiles at the lie. {menace} knows now how thin the walls are.

options.label: Send them off with a warning

success.text: The envoy goes white and spurs away. The town watches from the walls, and cheers.

failure.text: The envoy laughs and spits in the ford.

ignored.text: The rider waits a day and goes. Out in the hills, {menace} takes the silence for fear.

stories.title: The host of {menace} is on the road

stages.text: Scouts say the host of {menace} will camp tonight at the ford below {town}. There is still time to do something about it.

options.label: Lead a sally against the camp

critical.text: You fall on the camp in the small hours and burn half its wagons. You're home before dawn, and the bells ring for you.

success.text: You strike the camp at moonset and are back behind the walls by first light. The host will march on lighter.

partial.text: You do real harm to the camp, and bring back wounded.

failure.text: The camp was waiting for you. You get most of your people back.

fumble.text: It goes wrong from the first step. The host jeers at the walls all night.

success.text: You break the old weir at midnight, and the river does the rest. The host must find another crossing.

failure.text: The weir holds against everything you throw at it.

success.text: By morning the camp believes the town has a dragon. Deserters stream off into the hills.

failure.text: Your false rumours never reach the camp's fires.

options.label: Ring the bells and man the walls

success.text: No tricks tonight: every hand to the walls, and the town sleeps a little easier for it.

stages.text: While the host searches for a crossing, a deserter from the ranks of {menace} comes to the gate, offering its order of march for a pardon.

success.text: The deserter is genuine. The heroes know now where the host is weakest.

failure.text: It was a ruse: the false order of march costs the town half a day.

success.text: The host sees what {town} does with its kind.

failure.text: The town is sickened by it.

ignored.text: The deserter slips away in the night.
Nobody stops them. The host camps at the ford and sings all night, and the town listens.

stages.text: Smoke at dawn over the outlying farms. Raiders of {menace} have driven off the cattle, and the farmers want them back.

success.text: You find the cattle in a gully, and the raiders guarding them run.

failure.text: The trail goes cold in the rocks, and an arrow from the heights wounds one of your riders.

success.text: The farmers band together and bring half the herd home themselves.

failure.text: The farmers go home, and the herd is gone.

options.label: Pay the farmers for their loss

success.text: Gold won't bring the cattle back, but the farmers know the hall stands with them.

ignored.text: The farmers count their losses and curse the hall.

stages.text: The lamps of {god} burned blue all night at the shrine, and the townsfolk want to know what it means.

success.text: A sign of favour, you tell them, and the shrine is full by evening.

failure.text: Your reading convinces nobody, the priests least of all.

options.label: Call it a blessing and throw a feast

success.text: The town feasts under blue lamps, and talks of nothing else for days.

failure.text: The feast is a damp affair, and the lamps go out halfway through.

options.label: Say it is only marsh gas

success.text: The sensible folk nod. The priests don't.

failure.text: Marsh gas, in a stone shrine? Nobody believes you.

ignored.text: The lamps burn yellow again by the next night, and the talk turns to the mayor's silence.

stages.text: A peddler has turned up a crown-piece stamped with the sign of {power}. Collectors would pay well for it, and the old folk say such things carry old grudges.

critical.text: It is the real thing, and a rare one. A collector in the south pays a fortune.

success.text: You know the mint and the reign. The town buys it cheap and sells it dear.

failure.text: It's a fake, and the town paid for it.

success.text: An old blessing, not a curse. You give it to the shrine, and sell the peddler's other trinkets.

failure.text: Something cold looks back at you out of the metal. You sleep badly for a week.

success.text: You get it for a song and sell it for a choir.

failure.text: The peddler knows what he has.

ignored.text: The peddler takes the crown-piece south.

stories.title: A child lost in the woods

stages.text: The cooper's daughter went out for mushrooms yesterday and hasn't come home. Her mother is at the hall door.

success.text: You find her by the brook at dusk, cold and cross and quite safe.

failure.text: The search finds nothing. She walks home the next morning, half frozen.

success.text: The old hound has her scent in a moment.

failure.text: The hounds chase a deer for an hour. She's found at dawn.

options.label: Ask a hero to find her

success.text: A hero has her home by supper, on their shoulders.

ignored.text: She finds her own way home after two cold nights, and her mother has things to say about the mayor.

stages.text: A crowd at the granary door is shouting about the price of bread, and someone has brought a torch.

success.text: You stand on a barrel and talk them home, one promise at a time.

partial.text: They go home, with a sack or two of grain each.

failure.text: The granary door gives way. By morning the stores are thinner and tempers no better.

options.label: Buy a wagon of grain from the river barges

success.text: The wagon rolls in at noon, and the crowd cheers it to the granary.
The torch goes out. The crowd goes home, muttering.

failure.text: The crowd boos you off the steps.

ignored.text: The granary is broken into in the night.

stages.text: A drunk at {tavern} is selling a map to {site}, where he swears his grandfather saw lights under the hill.

success.text: The landmarks are real. The town buys the map for the price of his supper.

failure.text: It looks like nonsense to you, and you buy it anyway, out of pity.

success.text: The map is smudged, but the hill is on it.
By the fourth ale he's told you the way for free.

failure.text: He falls asleep halfway through the story.

ignored.text: He sells the map to a passing tinker.

stages.text: Folk without homes have raised a camp of hides and sailcloth by the river. The neighbours want it gone, and the camp wants a roof.

success.text: A few doors open, a few hands are hired, and the camp shrinks by half.

failure.text: Nobody has room to spare, or so they say.

success.text: A building bee by the river, with a fiddler and a cauldron of stew. Two cabins go up by dark.

failure.text: Three people come, and one of them is the fiddler.

success.text: The camp moves on downriver. The neighbours are pleased, and nobody else is.

failure.text: The camp won't move, and the whole town watches you fail to move it.

ignored.text: The camp stays, and so do the complaints.

stages.text: Three households are down with a sweating fever, and a fourth this morning. The herbwife says it came up the river.

success.text: Willow bark, clean water and long nights. The fever breaks in every house.

partial.text: The fever breaks, but the herbs and the nursing cost the town.

failure.text: The fever is beyond your herbs.

success.text: The lanes are closed and kept closed. The fever burns out where it started.

failure.text: People slip through the cordon at night.

success.text: The priests of {god} go house to house, and the fever goes with them.

stages.text: The fever has jumped the lanes. Doors are chalked, and people are blaming strangers.

success.text: A fouled well by the tannery. You seal it, and the fever fades within the week.

failure.text: You never find the source. The fever runs its course, and takes its toll.

success.text: Whether it's {god} or the rest, the town comes through, and remembers who sat with them.

failure.text: The prayers bring comfort, and nothing else.

options.label: Send for a healer at any price

success.text: A healer from the south arrives in a lacquered coach, and earns every coin.

ignored.text: The fever runs through the town and burns itself out.
The fever burns itself out, but not before half the town has had it.

stages.text: {petitioner}, a {trade}, stands before you with mud to the knee: a neighbour has moved the boundary stone between their plots by a full stride, and swears it was always there.

success.text: You pace it out with both of them and an old ox-goad for a rod. The stone goes back, and even the neighbour grudgingly shakes on it.

failure.text: You judge for the neighbour, and the whole street knows you judged wrong.

success.text: Half a stride each and a jug of cider to seal it. Nobody is happy, which is how you know it's fair.

failure.text: Neither will give an inch, and both blame you.

success.text: Twenty gold for a stride of mud. The stone stays where it is, and so does the peace.

ignored.text: {petitionerName} moves the stone back by night, and the neighbour moves it again. The feud runs on.

stages.text: {petitioner} begs you to break the indenture on their youngest, bound for seven years to a master in {ward} who feeds the apprentices thin gruel and works them by lamplight.

options.label: Shame the master into releasing the child

success.text: Before half the guild you ask whether this is how a master keeps faith. The indenture is torn up by sundown.

failure.text: The master quotes the indenture back to you, clause by clause, and he is within his rights.

success.text: The master has been short-weighting the guild's flour. The indenture is the least of his troubles now.

failure.text: His books are clean, or cleaned. Nothing to be done.

success.text: Forty gold, and the child walks home with {petitionerName}. The street will remember it.

ignored.text: Nobody steps in. {petitionerName} takes the child and the family takes the south road.

stages.text: {petitioner} brings a petition with forty marks on it: the stallholders want the market tolls lifted. They swear the town will earn it back twice over in trade and settlers.

options.label: Lift the tolls for the season

success.text: Tolls are lifted. Carts come in from three valleys, and the treasury tightens its belt.

options.label: Make the guild pay the tolls instead

success.text: The merchants' guild grumbles and pays the stallholders' tolls out of its own chest, to be seen to.

partial.text: The guild pays half, and you find the rest in the treasury.

failure.text: The guild refuses, and the stallholders saw you ask and fail.

success.text: The tolls stay. The stallholders take down their petition and some take down their stalls.

ignored.text: The petition goes unanswered. The stallholders take it as an answer.

stages.text: {petitioner} lost their spouse on the wall last month, a watch guard who held a gate alone. Now there is rent due and three children to feed, and the watch's pay died on the wall too.

options.label: Grant the watch's families a pension

success.text: The council grants a pension to every family the watch has lost. The watch stands a little straighter.

options.label: Ask the temple to take them in

success.text: The priests of {god} find the family rooms and work in the temple kitchens.

failure.text: The temple is full to the rafters with its own poor.

success.text: You tell the story of the gate at the market cross, and the hat comes back heavy.

failure.text: A few coppers, and some very hard looks at the town's purse.

ignored.text: Nobody answers. {petitionerName} sells what can be sold and leaves.

stages.text: {petitioner} hasn't slept a night through since spring: {tavern} roars till dawn, and the gutters are a disgrace. The neighbours want a curfew.

success.text: The taps close at the evening bell. The neighbours sleep, and the drinkers grumble on the way home.
The landlord shutters the windows, moves the dicing to the cellar and sweeps the lane. Peace, of a sort.

failure.text: The landlord laughs and pours you a drink.

success.text: You tell {petitionerName} that a frontier town is a loud town. They don't take it well.

ignored.text: Nothing is done. {petitionerName} takes to throwing slops at the drinkers.

stages.text: The carters of {ward} have sent a delegation: the road in is axle-deep after every rain, and they want it drained and gravelled before the next.

success.text: Ditches, gravel and a stone culvert. Carts roll in dry, and the building sites get their timber on time.

options.label: Raise a work gang from the ward

success.text: The ward turns out with spades on a feast day, and you dig the first ditch yourself.

failure.text: Twelve people come. The road is muddier for their trampling.

success.text: You find the old drove road on higher ground. It needs little more than clearing.

failure.text: Your better line runs straight into a bog.

ignored.text: The road stays a bog, and the carters stop coming.

stages.text: {petitioner} speaks for the farms: blight in the low fields and a wet summer. They ask that the town's tithe be eased for the harvest, or some will not see the spring.

success.text: The tithe is eased for the season. The farms bring in every last sheaf, and the treasury goes without.

options.label: Check their claims in the fields

success.text: You walk the low fields: real blight, but only in two. Those two are let off, the rest pay.

failure.text: You can't tell blight from bad husbandry, and the farmers see it.

success.text: The tithe stands. The farms pay, and remember.

ignored.text: Nobody answers, and the farmers hold back their tithe anyway.

stages.text: A column of carts and walking wounded is at the gate: families burned out of their villages by {menace}. They beg to be let in. The town's stores are what they are, and nobody can say who among them {menace} has sent.

success.text: The gates open. The town makes room, and stretches its stores to the breaking point.
You walk the column and choose: smiths, masons, a midwife. The rest are given bread and pointed south.

partial.text: You choose well enough, but one of them slips away by night with a map of the walls.

failure.text: You choose the wrong ones: within a week, a fire in the granary and two of them gone.

success.text: The gates stay shut. The column camps a night below the walls, then moves on into the dark.

ignored.text: While the council argues the column moves on, and not all of it reaches the next town.

stages.text: The refugees you took in have crowded into {ward}, and the old families mutter about strange gods and stranger cooking. The newcomers ask for a voice on the ward's moot.

options.label: Give them a quarter and a voice

success.text: The newcomers get their seat on the moot and a street of their own. Their cousins start coming up the road.
A feast on the ward green, each side cooking for the other. By midnight they're arguing about weddings.

failure.text: The feast ends in a brawl over the last of the mutton.

options.label: Tell them to keep their heads down

success.text: The newcomers keep their heads down. Some of them keep walking.

ignored.text: Nothing is done, and the two sides settle it in the lanes.

stages.text: The merchants' guild lays a chest on the council table: three hundred gold, and more each season, for the sole right to trade in {ward}. Every other stall there would answer to them.

success.text: The chest goes into the treasury. The guild's men take down every other stall in the ward by Friday.

options.label: Bargain them down to a fair charter

success.text: A charter, not a monopoly: the guild keeps a fair share of the ward's trade and pays well for the seal.

partial.text: They take the charter at a lower price, and grumble about it.

failure.text: The guild takes its chest and its custom to the next town.

success.text: You push the chest back across the table. The stallholders of {ward} hear of it by evening.

ignored.text: While you dither, the guild buys up the ward's stalls one by one anyway.

stages.text: Having bought one ward, the merchants' guild now wants the {seat} for its master, and hints that the gold could stop.

success.text: You tear up the guild's monopoly before the council. The guild master goes white and says nothing.

failure.text: The guild's lawyers find the pact unbreakable, and the master laughs on the steps of the hall.

success.text: The guild master takes his seat. The council's votes start to come out the guild's way.

options.label: Play the guild against the council

success.text: A word here and a rumour there, and the guild and the {seat} are at each other's throats instead of yours.

failure.text: Both sides find out what you told the other.

ignored.text: The guild takes the silence as consent and buys the seat itself.

stories.title: The captain asks for a levy

stages.text: {menace} has been seen on every ridge this month. The captain of the watch wants a levy: every able hand drilled on the green at dawn, the building sites be hanged.

success.text: The levy is called. Spears on the green at dawn, and empty scaffolds by noon.

options.label: Drill them yourself in the evenings

success.text: You lead the drill after the day's work, and the town learns to hold a line without losing a day's building.

failure.text: By the third evening half the drill is in the tavern, and the captain is furious.

options.label: Trust the walls and the watch

success.text: No levy. The captain salutes, and says nothing, loudly.

ignored.text: No answer comes. The captain drills those who will turn up.

stages.text: A crowd has dragged {petitioner} to the well, a {trade} who keeps herbs and talks to crows. The cows are dry and two children have the cough, and the crowd wants a reckoning.

success.text: You find the cowman's been watering the milk and the cough came in with a peddler. The crowd goes home ashamed.

partial.text: You find enough doubt to send the crowd home, though not to change their minds.

failure.text: You find nothing either way, and the crowd decides for itself.

options.label: Stand between them and the crowd

success.text: You stand at the well with your chain of office on and dare them. One by one, they go home.

failure.text: The crowd shoves past you.

options.label: Give the crowd what it wants

success.text: You step aside. {petitionerName} is driven out of {town} with stones at their back.

stages.text: The crowd has a rope and a cart. {petitionerName} is looking at you.

options.label: Bundle them out the back way

success.text: A back door, a borrowed cloak and a cart of turnips. {petitionerName} is three miles off before the crowd knows.

failure.text: You're caught at the gate with the witch in your cart.

success.text: You turn away. The town has its reckoning, and some of it will never quite meet your eye again.

ignored.text: Nobody stops the crowd.

stages.text: A crow taps at your window with a bundle tied to its leg: dried herbs and a note in a cramped hand. "For what you did at the well."

options.label: Take the herbs to the sick

success.text: The herbs break three fevers in the lanes. You never say where they came from.

failure.text: You can't make head or tail of the herbs, but you keep the note.

success.text: You burn it in the grate. Some debts are better left unpaid.

ignored.text: The crow waits, then flies off with its bundle.

stories.title: A hoard in the hungry winter

stages.text: The cellars are emptying, and the town knows a grain merchant has a full granary behind the tannery. He'll sell, at four times the autumn price.

success.text: The watch breaks the granary doors. The town eats, the merchant rides off swearing, and every trading house hears of it.
You pay. The merchant smiles and the town eats.

options.label: Make him sell at a fair price

success.text: You remind him what crowds do to hoarders in hungry winters. He sells at the autumn price and thanks you for the advice.

failure.text: He calls your bluff and doubles the price.

success.text: Every household draws a measured share until the thaw. Nobody starves, and nobody is happy.

ignored.text: The merchant sells to whoever pays most, and the poor go hungry.

stages.text: {hero} has been playing {tavern} for their supper, and the room fills whenever they do. They ask whether {town} would keep a bard of its own.

options.label: Give them the stage and a purse

success.text: {heroName} plays {tavern} every night now. Folk walk in from the farms to hear them.
You know the words, more or less. The room roars, and {heroName} is {town}'s own.

failure.text: The room laughs at you, not with you. {heroName} plays on, but not for the town.

critical.text: You know every word and hit every note. The room roars, and {town} has a bard of its own.

partial.text: Your voice cracks on the high note. The room laughs with you, mostly, and {heroName} stays.

options.label: Ask them for a ballad of the founding

success.text: You tell them the old stories, and they make a ballad of it. By the week's end every tavern sings it.

failure.text: You get the dates wrong. The ballad is about somebody else's town.

options.label: Say the town has no gold for minstrels

success.text: {heroName} bows, a little too low, and plays on for their supper.

ignored.text: {heroName} plays on for their supper, then takes the road for a week.

stages.text: {heroName}'s new song is about {councillor}, the {seat}, and a goat. All {town} is singing it.

success.text: You sing the goat's verse louder than anyone. The town loves it; {councillor} does not.

options.label: Ask the bard to drop the verse

success.text: {heroName} grumbles and writes a new verse about the weather.

failure.text: {heroName} plays it twice as loud the next night.

options.label: Answer with a verse of your own

success.text: Your verse about the bard's own goat goes round the taverns. Honours even.

failure.text: Your verse scans badly, and now there are two songs about the hall.

critical.text: Your verse is better. The whole hall laughs, even {councillor}.

success.text: The song stops. So does {heroName}'s playing for the town.

ignored.text: The song runs its course. {councillor} doesn't come to the tavern for a month.

stages.text: {hero} kneels at the gate at dawn and asks to swear an oath to {town}. A paladin's oath binds both ways, and the words are yours to choose.

options.label: Swear the Oath of the Shield: hold the walls

success.text: 'While I stand, the gate stands.' {heroName} rises sworn to the walls.

options.label: Swear the Oath of Mercy: tend the weak

success.text: 'No one in this town goes hungry while I eat.' {heroName} rises sworn to the poor lanes.

options.label: Swear the Oath of Vengeance: hunt what preys on us

success.text: 'Whatever comes for {town} will find me first.' The town sleeps a little easier, and {heroName} a little less.

options.label: Swear them to the walls before the altar

success.text: The priests ring every bell, and {god} seems to listen. {heroName} swears to the walls, and the whole town comes out to watch.

failure.text: You stumble over the rite, and the priests exchange looks. The oath is sworn all the same.

options.label: Tell them the town needs no oaths

success.text: {heroName} rises, unsworn, and does not kneel at that gate again.

ignored.text: Nobody from the hall comes to the gate. {heroName} rises unsworn.

stages.text: The watch has caught a boy stealing bread, and {hero} stands between him and the stocks. 'My oath is to the weak,' they say. 'Put me there instead.'

success.text: The boy goes free into {heroName}'s keeping. Some say the law has gone soft; more say the oath is real.
His mother is sick and the family's stores are empty. You send bread to the house, and the boy to {heroName} as a squire.

failure.text: The boy lies to you, then lies again. You give him to the oath anyway.

options.label: Let the law take its course

success.text: The boy goes to the stocks. {heroName} watches, then walks out through the gate, and the oath is broken.

ignored.text: The watch and the paladin stare at each other until the boy slips away.

stages.text: {faction} has offered {hero} a seat at its table in the cellar. {heroName} has come to you first, which is more than most rogues would.

options.label: Take the seat and keep their knives off the town

success.text: {heroName} sits down with {faction}. There are fewer thefts in the market, and a fat envelope reaches the hall every week.

options.label: Take the seat and tell me everything

success.text: {heroName} smiles the smile of a long career. Within a week you know who sits at that table, and the watch is starting to.

failure.text: {faction} smells it. {heroName} is shown the door with a cut across the cheek.

fumble.text: Someone talked. {heroName} is pulled out of the millrace at dawn, alive, barely.

options.label: Ask them to name names to the watch

success.text: {heroName} sighs and writes a list. The watch has names now.

failure.text: 'I'm a thief, not a snitch.' {heroName} won't, and resents you for asking.

success.text: {heroName} shrugs. The cellar door stays shut to them, for now.

ignored.text: {heroName} takes the seat without asking you again.

stages.text: {faction} wants something for the quiet it keeps: {hero} is to see the watch walks the other way while a caravan's strongbox goes missing.

success.text: The strongbox goes missing. A share of it turns up at the town hall in a flour sack.

options.label: Have {heroName} talk them out of it

success.text: {heroName} reminds them who keeps the watch off their backs. They pick another caravan, in another town.

failure.text: They don't listen. The strongbox goes, and the town gets nothing for it.

options.label: Spring a trap with the watch

success.text: The watch is waiting by the strongbox. Two of the guild's best are taken, and {heroName}'s seat at the table goes cold.

failure.text: The guild smells the trap and stays home. {heroName} is not welcome at the table again.

ignored.text: The strongbox goes missing, and nobody asks the hall.

stages.text: {hero} watched the militia drill on the green and laughed out loud. Now they offer to teach them properly, for a modest wage.

success.text: {heroName} has the militia on the green at dawn, shield to shield. They grumble, and they get better.

options.label: Spar with them on the green first

success.text: You hold your own for three passes. {heroName} grins and takes the job.

failure.text: You end up in the mud. {heroName} takes the job out of pity.

critical.text: You put {heroName} on their back, once. The militia talks of nothing else, and {heroName} takes the job laughing.

options.label: Say the militia will do as it is

success.text: {heroName} shrugs and goes back to their ale.

ignored.text: {heroName} stops watching the drills.

stages.text: {hero} has challenged anyone in {town} to lift the millstone in the square. Nobody can, and {heroName} is getting bored, and loud.

success.text: Wrestling, stone-throwing, a tug of war across the millpond. {heroName} wins all of it, then spends the month hauling beams for the builders to show off.
You get it to your knees, which is further than anyone else. {heroName} slaps your back and offers to haul for the builders.

failure.text: The stone wins. {heroName} is kind about it, which is worse.

critical.text: You lift it. Nobody, least of all you, knows how. {heroName} roars with delight and swears to haul for you.

options.label: Put them to work at the building sites

success.text: 'Heavier than the millstone?' They are. {heroName} hauls them for fun.

failure.text: 'I am not a mule.' {heroName} storms off.

ignored.text: {heroName} lifts the stone at last, and drops it through the well cover.

stages.text: {hero} asks leave to serve at {temple}: to preach on rest days or, if the town would rather, to tend the sick in the poorer lanes.

success.text: {heroName} preaches every rest day, and {temple} is fuller than it has been in years.

options.label: Tend the sick in the lanes

success.text: {heroName} goes door to door with salves and prayers. The poor lanes bless the mayor's name.

options.label: Lead the first rite with them

success.text: You know the litany by heart. {god} has two voices in {temple} now.

failure.text: You lose your place in the litany. {heroName} finishes it for you.

ignored.text: {heroName} preaches anyway, to the pigeons.

stages.text: {hero} has found an old oak grove by the river, where the woodcutters mean to start next. They ask the town to spare it, and say the land will thank it.

success.text: The axes go elsewhere. {heroName} keeps the grove, and the fields downriver come up greener.

options.label: Let them choose which trees fall

success.text: You walk the wood together and agree on every tree. {heroName} becomes the town's woodward.

failure.text: You can't tell an oak from an ash. {heroName} chooses alone and doesn't think much of you.

success.text: The grove comes down in a week. {heroName} watches every tree fall.

ignored.text: The woodcutters reach the grove before anyone decides.

stages.text: {hero} has walked every road out of {town} and says nobody is watching them. They have also found tracks out past the old roads that they don't like.

options.label: Make them warden of the roads

success.text: {heroName} walks the roads with a horn at their belt. Carters feel safer, and more of them come.
{heroName} draws you a map in the dust. There is something out at {site}.

failure.text: The tracks lead into a bog and out of your understanding.

options.label: Do both, and pay them well

success.text: {heroName} takes the horn and the purse, and comes back with a map: something is out at {site}.

ignored.text: {heroName} keeps what they found to themselves.

stages.text: Every dawn {hero} moves slow as water through the forms in the square, and a crowd of apprentices has started copying them before work.

options.label: Give them the old granary for a school

success.text: The granary fills before sunrise. The apprentices come to work calmer, and fight less in the taverns.
You keep up, mostly. The town sees its mayor at dawn in the square and likes it.

failure.text: You pull something in your back and limp for a week.

partial.text: You fall over twice. The apprentices love it.

options.label: Ask them to train the watch

success.text: {heroName} teaches the watch to take a club from a drunk without breaking either.

ignored.text: {heroName} keeps to the forms alone. The apprentices drift back to bed.

stages.text: Wild magic got loose from {hero} in the market: the fountain ran with wine for an hour, a cart floated off over the roofs, and somebody's goat is talking.

success.text: You make a joke of it, and the market laughs with you. {heroName} is grateful.

failure.text: Nobody hears you over the goat.

success.text: Free wine from the fountain! The town drinks to the sorcerer.

options.label: Put the spark to work in the forges

success.text: With your notes and {heroName}'s nerve, the smiths' fires burn hotter than coal can make them.

failure.text: The experiment sets the smithy roof alight. {heroName} singes their eyebrows putting it out.

critical.text: You work out what set it off, and how to set it off on purpose. The smiths have never had such fire.

success.text: {heroName} goes, red-faced. The market is calmer and the sorcerer is not.

ignored.text: The goat talks for a week. Nobody likes what it says.

stages.text: {hero}'s patron spoke through them in the night, in a voice that was not theirs: it will fill {town}'s coffers, if {town} will remember its name.

success.text: Gold is found in the old well by morning, and more every week after. Nobody likes to draw water there now.
You haggle it down to a smaller name in a smaller place. The gold still comes.

failure.text: The patron does not haggle. Every candle in town goes out at once.

critical.text: The patron laughs, a sound like ice cracking, and pays without a price.

options.label: Have the priests drive it out

success.text: The priests sing until dawn, and the voice goes quiet. {heroName} sleeps through the night for the first time in months.

failure.text: The priests' candles burn blue, and the voice laughs at them.

success.text: '{town} remembers no name but its own.' {heroName} looks relieved, and a little afraid.

ignored.text: The voice stops asking. Nobody knows if that is good.

stages.text: {hero}'s patron wants its due. Its name is to be carved over the town gate, so that all who walk beneath it know whose town this is.

success.text: It is carved. Children cross the road rather than walk under it.
You find the clause the patron didn't think you'd read. The pact breaks with a sound like a cracked bell. The gold stops, and so do the nightmares.

failure.text: The pact breaks, but not cleanly. {heroName} screams for an hour, and the old well runs black.

success.text: {heroName} speaks into the dark for a whole night. The patron settles for its name scratched under a bridge.

failure.text: The patron does not like being bargained with by its own servant.

ignored.text: The name appears over the gate by itself one morning, carved deep.

stages.text: {hero} wants to open a school in {town}: letters and numbers for every child, 'and a little arcana, for the bright ones.'

success.text: The school opens in a loft over the market. Within a season the clerks are quicker and the builders read plans.

options.label: Ask for wards on the walls instead

success.text: {heroName} sighs, and sets wards into the gatehouse stones instead.

options.label: Talk magic with them over supper

success.text: They like you. The school opens, and you teach one class a week.

failure.text: {heroName} corrects you, then corrects you again.

critical.text: You argue about the weave all night and both learn something. The school opens with you on its board.

success.text: {heroName} closes their book with a snap.

ignored.text: {heroName} takes pupils of their own, for coin.

stages.text: {hero} has stood a watch at the gate every night this month, unpaid and unasked. Now they ask for the keys, and the right to say who comes in after dark.

success.text: {heroName} hangs the keys at their belt and is not seen to sleep. Nobody comes in after dark that {heroName} has not looked at.

options.label: Have them walk the outer wards instead

success.text: {heroName} walks the lanes beyond the walls with a lantern every night. The newer wards sleep easier.

options.label: Test them at the gate yourself

success.text: You ask the questions a gatekeeper should ask, and they know every answer. The keys are theirs.

failure.text: You ask the wrong questions, and {heroName} answers them politely. The keys are theirs anyway.

options.label: Leave the gate to the watch

success.text: {heroName} hands back a key they had copied, and stops coming to the gate.

ignored.text: {heroName} keeps the night watch at the gate anyway, unpaid and unthanked.

stages.text: {hero} has spread a half-finished map across a tavern table: every road, ford and ruin within three days of {town}, with a great blank in the middle. They want a room to finish it in.

options.label: Give them a map room in the town hall

success.text: The map grows across a whole wall. Settlers come to the hall to find their way, and one blank fills in: {site}.
The old charters name a place nobody remembered: {site}. {heroName} draws it in and asks to stay on.

failure.text: The charters are mostly about sheep.

options.label: Buy the map as it stands

success.text: You pay for the map. {heroName} takes the coin to another town's tavern.

ignored.text: {heroName} rolls the map up and takes it on the road.

stages.text: {hero} has brought back a fragment of an old reliquary from a tomb. It is warm to the touch and, late at night, it whispers. They want to know if {town} will house it.

success.text: The fragment is set under glass at the temple, and {heroName} keeps it. Pilgrims come to hear it whisper.
It whispers of old powers and older debts. You come away wiser, and {heroName} stays on to keep it.

failure.text: It whispers your name back to you, and you don't sleep for three nights.

critical.text: It names a prayer the priests had lost, and the town is the better for knowing it. {heroName} stays on to keep it.

success.text: A collector from the Free Ports pays well and asks no questions. {heroName} thinks you sold something you shouldn't have.

ignored.text: {heroName} keeps it under their bed. The whispering spreads to the next room.

stages.text: {hero} has been brewing in the back of the apothecary between delves, and the midwives swear by their salves. They offer to brew for the whole town, if the town will have a witch.

success.text: {heroName} brews by the apothecary fire and nobody calls them a witch to their face. Fevers break sooner.

options.label: Ask them to bless the fields

success.text: You walk the furrows with them at dusk, and they sing to the seed. The harvest comes up strong.

failure.text: You trample the seedlings they just sang over. They bless the fields anyway, and sigh at you.

success.text: {heroName} packs their jars quietly. The midwives are angry with you.

ignored.text: {heroName} brews for whoever knocks at the back door.

stages.text: The caravan master from {settlement} swears the town's market weighers have been shorting {people} a pound in every ten, and wants it made good before the next caravan loads.

options.label: Weigh it out in front of them

success.text: You test every weight in the market before both sides. Two are light: you smash them, and the caravan master shakes your hand.

failure.text: The weights look true to you. The caravan master does not believe you.

success.text: A cup of the good wine and a promise of a fair scale. The caravan master leaves mollified.

failure.text: The caravan master takes your charm for an admission.

options.label: Make it good from the treasury

success.text: Thirty gold for a pound in every ten. The caravan master is satisfied, and the weighers are watched.

ignored.text: Nobody answers the caravan master, who tells {settlement} that {town} cheats.

stages.text: The watch has found barrels on the {settlement} caravan that were never weighed or taxed: smugglers are riding with the town's own drovers.

success.text: You let the next caravan load, then open every barrel at the gate. Three smugglers, a cart of contraband and a heavy fine.

failure.text: Somebody warns them. The next caravan is spotless, and so is the one after.

options.label: Take a cut and say nothing

success.text: The smugglers pay the town handsomely to look the other way, and nobody asks where the money came from.

failure.text: Word gets out that the mayor takes a cut from smugglers.

fumble.text: {people} find out first, and want nothing to do with a town that runs contraband.

success.text: You send word down the road, and {people} catch the smugglers at their end. They think the better of {town} for it.

ignored.text: The smuggling goes on until {people} catch it themselves, and blame the town.

stages.text: {people} ask to keep an envoy house in {town}: a roof, a flag over the door and a seat at the market moot. The council fears spies.

success.text: The envoy house opens with a feast, and {people} send their best to live in it.
You grant the house and keep an eye on its guests. They are what they say, and you make friends of them.

failure.text: Your watchers are clumsy, and the envoy notices.

success.text: No envoy house: {people} take the refusal politely, and remember it.

ignored.text: The request sits unanswered on the council table until {people} withdraw it.

stages.text: {people} propose a marriage: the heir of their first house and the {seat}'s youngest. It would bind {settlement} to {town} in all but name, and the {seat} is not sure.

options.label: Hold a wedding they will sing of

success.text: Three days of feasting, a bridge of flowers and every bell in town, and {settlement} goes home kin.

options.label: Talk the {seat} round to a modest match

success.text: A small wedding and a large dowry: {people} are honoured, and the {seat} is content.

partial.text: The match goes ahead, but the {seat} sulks through it.

failure.text: The {seat} refuses outright, and {people} take it as an insult.

success.text: You decline with every courtesy, and {people} take it well, outwardly.

ignored.text: The proposal is left to gather dust, and {people} find another match.

stages.text: The caravan from {settlement} brings a whole troupe this summer: merchants, players and a dancing bear. They ask for a pitch on the green.

success.text: The green fills with their stalls, and the town spends a happy week buying things it doesn't need.

options.label: Charge them a fair pitch fee

success.text: They pay a fair fee and are glad to.

failure.text: They think the fee steep and pitch outside the walls instead.

ignored.text: Nobody gives them a pitch, so they sell from their carts and leave early.

stages.text: {hero} has come home from more roads than anyone in {town} can count, and asks the mayor for leave to stop. The old {class} would rather teach the young ones at the practice yard than bleed for one more bounty.

success.text: {heroName} hangs the sword over the practice yard gate. From now on every new blade in town learns from a master.
{heroName} grumbles, laughs and agrees to one more season.

failure.text: {heroName} stays, but resents it.

success.text: A fat purse and a new cloak: {heroName} stays, for now.

ignored.text: Nobody answers {heroName}, who takes it hard.

stages.text: The road brings {fallen} home on a bier, wrapped in a company cloak. The town turns out at the gate, and everyone is watching to see what the mayor will do for the fallen {fallenClass}.

options.label: A hero's funeral and a stone

success.text: Drums, torches and a carved stone by the gate. Heroes and townsfolk drink to {fallenName} until dawn.
The mayor's words carry, and the town remembers {fallenName} well.

failure.text: The words come out wrong, and the mourners shuffle home.

success.text: A plain grave in the yard behind the temple. The heroes in the taverns notice how little it took.

ignored.text: {fallenName} is buried without a word from the town hall.

stages.text: A widow and two thin children stand at the town hall door: the family {fallen} sent coin home to. With the {fallenClass} dead, the coin has stopped.

success.text: A purse each season, in {fallenName}'s name. Word spreads in the taverns that {town} looks after its own.

options.label: Find them work and a roof

success.text: A guildmaster owes the mayor a favour, and the family settle in town.

failure.text: Nobody will take them on, and they go back down the road.

success.text: The family go back down the road, and the heroes in the taverns see them go.

ignored.text: Nobody answers, and the family go back down the road.

stages.text: A child chased a dog through a grate and has not come back up. Their mother stands at the opening to {site}, calling down into the dark, and half the street has gathered with lanterns.

options.label: Send the watch down after them

success.text: The watch comes up filthy and grinning, the child on a sergeant's shoulders. They saw what lives down there, and drove it back.

failure.text: The watch finds the child, but one of them is bitten badly and things follow the lanterns back toward the grate.

options.label: Offer a reward to anyone who goes

success.text: A rat-catcher goes down for the purse and brings the child up blinking. The street cheers the mayor's coin.
The grate is chained. Nobody speaks to the mayor in that street for a long while.

ignored.text: No one comes. The street goes down with its own lanterns, and not all of them come back up.

stages.text: Diggers mending a drain under {town} have broken through into {site} and found a door sealed with old wax and older marks. Something on the far side knocks back when they knock.

options.label: Have a scholar read the marks

success.text: The marks are a binding, still holding. A little fresh wax and the right words, and the knocking stops.

failure.text: The scholar reads the marks aloud, and gets one word wrong. The knocking becomes scratching.

options.label: Brick it up and say nothing

success.text: A wall of new brick goes up in front of the old door. The diggers are paid to forget it.

options.label: Break it open for what lies beyond

success.text: Behind the door, an old treasury and an older skeleton. The coin goes to the town.

failure.text: The door gives, and whatever was behind it is gone into the dark before anyone sees it.

ignored.text: The diggers refuse to go back down. The knocking can be heard in the cellars above.

stories.title: The night-soil men won't go down

stages.text: The night-soil men of {town} have downed their shovels. They say things in {site} have been watching them work, and they will not go back without better pay or a guard.

success.text: Coin steadies their nerves. The drains run, and they keep an eye on the dark for the town.
The mayor walks the first stretch with them, lantern high. Shamed and cheered, they follow.

failure.text: They won't hear it. The town reeks for a week before they are paid off.

success.text: The drains back up and the streets smell. Down below, something likes the quiet.

ignored.text: The drains back up, and the stink drives folk from the low streets.

decrees.name: Market tolls lifted
decrees.text: No tolls at the market. Stallholders come from further off, settlers follow them, and the treasury feels it.

decrees.name: A pension for the watch's widows
decrees.text: The town keeps the families of the watch it lost. Folk sleep easier for it.

decrees.name: The tavern curfew
decrees.text: The taps close at the evening bell. The lanes are quieter and the town is crosser.

decrees.name: Mended roads
decrees.text: Drained and gravelled roads: carts reach the building sites, and the road brings more hopefuls.

decrees.name: The eased tithe
decrees.text: The farms keep more of the harvest this season, and work the harder for it.

decrees.name: The guild's monopoly
decrees.text: One guild sets the prices in the ward. The treasury takes its share; nobody else likes it.

decrees.name: The levy
decrees.text: Every able hand drills on the green at dawn. The building sites stand half empty.

decrees.name: Merchants keep away
decrees.text: Word went round the trading houses that this town seizes grain. Caravans take the long road.

decrees.name: A quarter for the newcomers
decrees.text: The refugees have a quarter and a voice of their own, and their cousins are coming up the road.

decrees.name: Winter rationing
decrees.text: Every household draws a measured share from the common stores until the thaw.

precedents.text: The gates were opened to the refugees, and the town took them in.
The gates stayed shut while refugees begged outside them.
The mayor sold a guild the trade of a ward.
A hedge-witch was given to the crowd.
The mayor stood between a hedge-witch and the crowd.
The mayor seized a merchant's hoard in the hungry winter.
The mayor made a paladin break their oath of mercy.
The town took a dark patron's gold.

callings.name: The town's bard
callings.text: Plays the tavern every night. Spirits rise, and the road hears of it.

callings.name: Oath of the Shield
callings.text: Sworn to the walls. Stronger at the gate, steadier in the lanes.

callings.name: Oath of Mercy
callings.text: Sworn to the weak. The poor lanes are kinder, and the gods notice.

callings.name: Oath of Vengeance
callings.text: Sworn to hunt what preys on the town. Dread ebbs; the town is a grimmer place.

callings.name: Go-between to the Quiet Hand
callings.text: Sits at the thieves' table. Their knives stay off the town, and an envelope comes every week.

callings.name: Informer in the Quiet Hand
callings.text: Sits at the thieves' table and tells the watch. The guild grows hotter until it is exposed.

callings.name: Drillmaster of the militia
callings.text: Drills the militia at dawn. The walls are better held.

callings.name: Strongarm of the works
callings.text: Hauls beams and stone for the builders, for fun. Building goes faster.

callings.name: Preacher at the temple
callings.text: Preaches every rest day. The town's god is honoured and the lanes are calmer.

callings.name: Healer of the poor
callings.text: Tends the sick in the poorer lanes, with salves the town pays for.

callings.name: Keeper of the grove
callings.text: Keeps the old grove. Fields come up greener; less timber is cut.

callings.name: Woodward
callings.text: Chooses which trees fall. The woods and the fields both do better.

callings.name: Warden of the roads
callings.text: Walks the roads with a horn. Carters and settlers feel safer coming.

callings.name: Teacher of the dawn forms
callings.text: Teaches the forms at dawn. Apprentices are calmer and fight less.

callings.name: Trainer of the watch
callings.text: Trains the watch to fight with open hands. Steadier walls, fewer broken heads.

callings.name: Spark of the forges
callings.text: Lights the smiths' fires with wild magic. More tools, and the odd scorched roof.

callings.name: The patron's tithe
callings.text: Gold from the old well every week. Dread grows, and the gods turn away.

callings.name: The town's sage
callings.text: Runs a school of letters and numbers. Clerks are quicker and builders read plans.

callings.name: Warder of the walls
callings.text: Sets wards in the gatehouse stones. The walls are harder to breach.

callings.name: Keeper of the gate keys
callings.text: Holds the gate keys. Nothing comes in after dark unseen.

callings.name: Lantern of the outer wards
callings.text: Walks the lanes outside the walls at night. The newer wards sleep easier.

callings.name: Keeper of the map room
callings.text: Keeps the great map in the town hall. Settlers find their way here, and the wilds seem smaller.

callings.name: Keeper of the whispering relic
callings.text: Keeps a whispering relic at the temple. Pilgrims and the gods come closer; so does something else.

callings.name: The town's herbalist
callings.text: Brews salves and draughts by the apothecary fire. Fevers break sooner.

callings.name: Blesser of the fields
callings.text: Sings to the seed at dusk. The harvest comes up strong.
